narrative:
The model predicted an 80.3% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by your academic performance during law school itself. Your ranking in the bottom decile of your class at the end of your third year was the single strongest reason the model expected you to fail. Your first-year ranking, which placed you in the lowest decile, was the second most important factor and pushed the prediction even further toward failure. These two early indicators of relative class standing outweighed every other piece of information the model considered.

Your high family income worked mildly in your favor, slightly lowering the predicted risk of failure. However, it was not nearly strong enough to overcome the impact of your class rankings. Your LSAT score of 37 and undergraduate GPA of 3.5 were actually slightly better than the averages of students who were accepted, yet they could not compensate for the clear signal coming from your law-school grades.

To improve your chances, you should focus on raising your academic performance to the middle of the class in any future coursework, retake the bar exam if possible after targeted preparation, or consider reapplying once you have stronger evidence of consistent academic success.
